rv.q: It’s just too bad nothing else in this rote retread comes close to the unpredictable energy of Annie’s almighty insanity.

"The challenge is to get someone who knows the story anxious all over again. And that they do. The box-office catnip is Willis, totally convincing in his first play since his early off-Broadway days…But the wow factor, the precision instrument that keeps propelling the story into psychologically unexpected corners, is Laurie Metcalf...
It’s a stunning performance, even if, in this oddly fear-free production, she provokes more pity than terror.
Nowhere this season on Broadway is there an acting gulf as wide between two leads than here.
Willis's weirdly narcotized and passive Broadway debut goes above and beyond the drugged, physically diminished circumstances of his character.
That is, he’s a wisecracking, sleepily charming stoic who occasionally flinches or roars when he is subjected to severe pain, but never, ever lets us see that he might be afraid.

Mr. Willis, who has shown a knack for offbeat originality in films like “Pulp Fiction” and “Mortal Thoughts,” here goes through the motions of these preparations with a generic gruff good humor and the air of someone who would just as soon be taking a nap.

But the lack of a zesty scene partner who is really going to challenge her and go for broke eventually seems to wear Metcalf down — it is like watching a two-hander with one of the hands shrouded in mist.
Willis’s line readings are flat, and he is atrociously slow at picking up Metcalf’s cues.
Willis, though well-cast (taciturn suffering has more or less become his thing), just doesn’t seem particularly endangered.
What this is, is a summer stock production (indeed, it was first produced at the Bucks County Playhouse) from somewhere on the Straw Hat circuit that ceased to exist at least three decades ago.
Nor is there any other reason to go to “Misery,” which has nothing else to offer save for the chance to get Mr. Willis’s autograph after the show.
I was always involved, and willing to wait as the set turned once again from bedroom to hallway to living room to the exterior.
MISERY on Broadway is a bit of tasty popcorn elevated to high art by an exceptional stage actor.

Every writer, even a lowly website theater critic, wants to have a “number 1 fan” – unless, of course, they’ve read Stephen King’s terrifying 1987 novel “Misery,” seen its Oscar-winning 1990 screen version, or now, viewed its highly effective Broadway adaptation (by William Goldman, the film’s screenwriter) at the Broadhurst Theatre.
As far as nights at the theater go, one could do a lot worse.
The resulting part thriller, part comic parody has just one or two really tense scenes but it's amusing to have you giggling at even Annie's most bizarre actions.
However, though the technical specs are excellent, the production suffers from a curious lack of tension.
Misery, the play, will be remembered for Bruce Willis’ mild Broadway debut and Laurie Metcalf’s bravura performance.

Those with a limited tolerance for such mockery - and sometimes gruesome antics (fans looking forward to a scene involving Paul’s ankles won’t be disappointed) -- may feel uncomfortable watching the fun this Misery has at the expense of both main characters.
A play like this is a kind of game; here, however, only one person on stage is playing for keeps.
Die-HARD? Die-easy is more like it.
Although it’s not a great acting vehicle for Willis, it does at least share that trait with his films.
Despite Metcalf's excellently maniacal Annie, the tension here is more discomfort than terror
Although he does manage some priceless blank stares, his acting registers as something close to a non-performance in a 1,100-seat Broadway house.
Unfortunately, it’s not just Paul’s legs that are hobbled here, it’s the entire show.
Frankly, this “Misery” doesn’t have enough over-the-top physical torture and mayhem to relieve its long spells of tedium.
It's not a bad time, but when you're a millisecond away from witnessing a brutal act and you and the people around you can barely stifle snickers, it's not exactly a good time, either.
Those who don’t see the humor are likely to find it a pointless star vehicle.
The other sad element that drags this production so far down that it barely has a pulse is the performance of Mr. Willis.
Except for an instant when Willis brashly flashes his nemesis the bird, he's so bland it's frightening.
What might seem creepy on film plays as silly and campy on stage.
Misery certainly is not miserable and it deserves to be seen.
The work is truly terrifying at moments but fails to keep the intensity throughout.
I actually ended up not minding the show at all.
Stephen King is known for his suspense, but this production lacks the energy of the source material.
As a play, “Misery” just seems ridiculous, over the top, and in the end, pointless.
It is not altogether a miserable experience — thanks to the superb Laurie Metcalf
We know Mr. Willis is a great superhero on the screen; unfortunately, he is one-dimensional on the stage.

Attempting to pull the wool over the eyes of some theater patrons who should know better than to be fooled by star casting, playing it for laughs, gimmicks and a cheesy script that has more holes than there are in a huge chunk of Swiss.

cn.t: Critics find this Stephen King adaptation largely lifeless, with Laurie Metcalf's electric performance as the deranged fan completely overshadowing Bruce Willis's stiff, disengaged Broadway debut—resulting in a thriller that lacks suspense.

sg.ra: Headout and TickPick both name Center Orchestra rows D-K as the house sweet spot; Broadhurst's mezzanine overhang does not begin cutting the stage picture until row K, so D-K sits entirely in front of the overhang line while still clearing the shallow front-row rake. SeatPlan editors specifically advise skipping rows A-C because the Broadhurst stage pushes action to the sides that front-row patrons miss.

Broadhurst's mezzanine overhang begins at row K and, per Headout and SeatPlan, 'visibly cuts into the top of the stage by row R' - specifically blocking projections and anything that plays high. The rake in these rear orchestra rows is also called out as shallow, compounding the loss of vertical stage picture.

SeatPlan specifically flags the Broadhurst's Left and Right Boxes as overhanging far-aisle orchestra seats around rows D-F, cutting off the corresponding side of the stage, and the three elevated boxes themselves 'sit at quite sharp angles' with unfixed chairs. Headout adds that double-digit seats near the aisle get only partial views of the stage.

Multiple sources (Headout, SeatPlan, NewYorkTheatreGuide) call Center Mezzanine rows A-B the second-best location in the house. The Broadhurst's front mezzanine ledge has no railing, so shorter patrons aren't blocked - a Broadhurst-specific quirk noted by both SeatPlan and Headout. Because there is no balcony above, front-mezz rows have zero overhang.

SeatPlan calls Center Mezzanine rows C-F the value pick - 'enough rake to see over the top of heads' at sub-premium pricing - and because Broadhurst has no balcony above, the rear mezzanine is not overhung itself. The back four rows are slightly shorter with a decent rake, and a Tripadvisor reviewer (Apr 2024) reported a 'crystal clear view' from the last row of the mezzanine.
